headline: Wisconsin GOP Senate leader Bradley open to talks on legal cannabis
dek: Incoming Wisconsin Senate Minority Leader Julian Bradley says he will look at a cannabis bill, as Democrats weigh a stand-alone bill or the 2027 budget.
key_points: Julian Bradley, the incoming Republican leader in Wisconsin's Senate, said this week he wants to see legalization language before taking a position, rather than ruling it out.
Democrats take an 18-15 Senate and 53-46 Assembly majority in January, with Governor-elect Crowley, and can pass a bill without Republican votes if they stay united.
Incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein said it is to be determined whether legalization comes as a separate bill or in the state budget.
Republicans blocked Democratic legalization bills for 13 straight years; the latest died on 23 March 2026.
body: Wisconsin's incoming Republican Senate leader has declined to rule out cannabis legalization, a small but notable shift in a state where his party has blocked every legalization bill for more than a decade. Senator Julian Bradley of New Berlin, chosen as Senate minority leader after Democrats won both chambers on 3 November, told reporters this week that lawmakers need to see the bill and its language before discussing it, Wausau Pilot & Review reported on 13 November.

Bradley stopped short of support, and he did not answer the outlet's follow-up questions. But the comment matters because Democrats now hold the votes to pass legalization themselves, and the shape of any bill, and whether it draws Republican votes, will decide how durable it is.

Democrats will start the 2027 session with an 18-15 majority in the Senate and a 53-46 majority in the Assembly, alongside Governor-elect Crowley, giving the party control of state government for the first time in 16 years, The Marijuana Herald reported. Incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer said on 10 November that legalization is a priority for her caucus and that Democrats hope to pass it in the coming year.

The open question is how. Asked whether legalization would come as a stand-alone bill or inside the next state budget, incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein said it was to be determined, according to Wausau Pilot & Review. Hesselbein told the Wisconsin Examiner her caucus would meet through November and December to settle priorities. A spokesman for Crowley did not answer questions about Neubauer's one-year timeframe.

As we reported on 12 November, Crowley has pitched cannabis revenue as one way to offset federal Medicaid cuts, which would favour putting legalization in the budget. A budget route can move faster and carry tax rates directly, but it also ties cannabis to every other spending fight.
> In Wisconsin the question is no longer whether Democrats can pass legalization. It is whether they write a bill Republicans can live with when power changes again.

Bradley said in a 2020 candidate interview that he opposed recreational marijuana, according to NORML's voter guide, which also records that he wanted medical cannabis to go through the same approval process as any other drug. His comments this week are a softer line, made in his first days as minority leader. He told reporters Republicans are prepared for life in the minority and want to work with Democrats on tax cuts and affordability, the Wisconsin Examiner reported, while promising to fight other Democratic priorities hard.

Democrats have proposed legalization in each of the last 13 years, all stopped by the Republican-controlled Legislature, Wausau Pilot & Review reported. The latest bill, introduced in February, would have let adults 21 and older possess cannabis, let people 18 and older possess it for medical use, and licensed production and sale; it died on 23 March. Outgoing Governor Tony Evers proposed decriminalization and a medical program in his budgets.

Public support is strong. A Marquette Law School poll from June 2025 found 67% of Wisconsin voters backed legalization, including 88% of Democrats and 79% of independents, while 56% of Republicans opposed it, according to the Herald. Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota all sell adult-use cannabis, and Hesselbein has argued Wisconsin is losing revenue to them.
## What it means for the industry

Wisconsin is one of the few states with no comprehensive medical cannabis program, so a law would create a market from scratch in a state bordered by three adult-use markets. For multistate operators in Illinois, Michigan and Minnesota, the design questions matter: whether the state licenses vertically integrated companies, sets caps, or favours local applicants. That last point connects to the residency case now before the US Supreme Court.

The new Legislature convenes in January 2027. Watch for Democrats' decision on a stand-alone bill versus the budget, the first draft text that Bradley says he wants to see, and whether any Senate Republicans sign on. When Crowley presents his first budget, watch whether it already counts cannabis revenue.
